architectural_implications.before: Agent plans expressed as natural-language text or ad-hoc prompting.
architectural_implications.consequence: Enables static inspection, permissioning, and deterministic replay, but sacrifices the generality of free-text plans.

architectural_implications.after: Orchestrated DAG of parallel computer-use sub-agents under a manager with a re-plan loop and summarization stage.
architectural_implications.before: Single monolithic agent or loosely chained role prompts.

architectural_implications.observation: Multi-agent decomposition is formalized as an explicit Manager → DAG → parallel CUA sub-agents → follow-up/replan → deliverables pipeline.

architectural_implications.after: Continuous plan revision triggered by environmental feedback and value/affordance estimates.
architectural_implications.before: Plan once, then execute blindly; failures surface only at task end.
architectural_implications.consequence: Adds a control-loop layer to agent runtimes that must decide when to commit vs. re-plan.
architectural_implications.observation: Re-planning and error detection become required runtime components rather than prompt tricks.

article_ideas.angle: Take the checkability/flexibility trade-off seriously and show which production mechanisms (static inspection, permission modes, deterministic replay) are impossible under free-text plans.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Daniel Fried
  • Channel: Graham Neubig
  • Main topic: Planning, Task Decomposition, and Multi-Agent Coordination in LLM Agents
  • Purpose: To educate students on how AI agents plan, decompose tasks into sub-goals, and coordinate in multi-agent workflows. The lecture covers planning, task decomposition, and multi-agent coordination for language model agents. It discusses how agents form representations of future work, the role of chain-of-thought, subtask decomposition, and modularity in agentic systems, comparing them with classical AI planning (STRIPS/PDDL) and highlighting trade-offs between planning upfront versus reactive execution.

Topic Map

Introduction to Planning and Task Decomposition

  • Explanation: Overview of planning as an agent's representation of future behavior, drawing on chain-of-thought and environmental feedback.
  • Key claims:
    • Plans must be revisable based on environmental feedback.
    • Planning bridges the gap between static instructions and dynamic execution.
  • Examples:
    • GPU workstation purchasing task involving multiple vendor searches, cluster compatibility checks, and procurement.
  • Terminology:
    • Planning
    • Task Decomposition
    • Chain-of-Thought
    • Multi-Agent System
  • Why it matters: Planning enables agents to handle long-horizon tasks and manage complex dependencies.

Chain-of-Thought as a Plan

  • Explanation: Examining how chain-of-thought generation serves as a primitive form of planning and extra computation for LLMs.
  • Key claims:
    • Chain-of-thought provides extra compute and a scratchpad for models.
    • Decomposing complex reasoning into sub-questions improves performance.
  • Examples:
    • Kojima et al. (2022) 'Let's think step by step' and Wang et al. (2023) decomposition approaches.
  • Terminology:
    • Chain-of-Thought
    • Decomposed Prompting
    • Least-to-Most Prompting
  • Why it matters: Understanding the foundation of planning in LLMs helps improve their reasoning capabilities.

Classical Planning vs. LLM Planning

  • Explanation: Comparing classical symbolic planning (STRIPS, PDDL) with implicit LLM planning.
  • Key claims:
    • Classical planning uses explicit predicates, preconditions, and effects.
    • LLM planning is implicit, leveraging vast pre-training knowledge rather than rigorous search.
  • Examples:
    • Blocks world domain with pick-up and put-down actions.
  • Terminology:
    • Classical Planning
    • STRIPS
    • PDDL
    • Preconditions
    • Effects
    • Implicit Planning
  • Why it matters: Highlights what is hard and what has changed when moving from symbolic AI to neural language agents.

Plan Representations and Workflows

  • Explanation: Discussing how plans are represented ranging from text, structured graphs, and code-based policies.
  • Key claims:
    • Code-based plans offer programmatic control and API calls.
    • Formal plans are checkable, while language plans are general.
  • Examples:
    • Cursor Plan Mode, Claude Code, and CodeX workflows.
  • Terminology:
    • Plan Representations
    • Code-Based Plans
    • Workflows
    • Permission Mode
  • Why it matters: Choosing the right plan representation affects checkability, flexibility, and execution success.

Modularity, Affordances, and Re-planning

  • Explanation: Exploring the decomposition of tasks across multiple specialized agents and the integration of feedback and value functions.
  • Key claims:
    • Separating planners from executors allows specialized model training.
    • Re-planning lets models adapt when execution reveals new information.
  • Examples:
    • SayCan affordance modeling and Voyager/Odysseys multi-agent architectures.
  • Terminology:
    • Modularity
    • Affordances
    • Value Functions
    • Re-planning
    • Execution Horizon
    • Overthinking
  • Why it matters: Structuring agents with modularity and re-planning improves success rates on long-horizon tasks.

Multi-Agent Coordination and Failures

  • Explanation: Analyzing multi-agent systems, fixed roles, handoffs, and long-horizon failure modes.
  • Key claims:
    • Stronger manager agents improve coordination and lift weaker workers.
    • Fixed multi-agent roles can suffer from rigid communication and context drops.
  • Examples:
    • Vending-Bench long-horizon task failures and OSWorld ablation studies.
  • Terminology:
    • Multi-Agent Coordination
    • Handoffs
    • Long-Horizon Failures
    • Vending-Bench
  • Why it matters: Identifies the limitations and pitfalls of multi-agent delegation and execution over extended periods.

Key Points

Planning is a moving target

  • Explanation: Agents must balance commitment to a course of action with flexibility to adapt to new environmental information.
  • Evidence: Agent tasks in dynamic environments like web browsing require continuous plan revision.
  • Practical implication: Agent design must incorporate mechanisms for error detection and re-planning.

Chain-of-Thought acts as a primitive plan

  • Explanation: Prompting models to think step-by-step or decompose tasks provides a scratchpad and extra compute before final execution.
  • Evidence: Studies like Least-to-Most Prompting show performance gains from subtask decomposition.
  • Practical implication: Use structured prompting or decomposition to handle multi-step reasoning tasks.

Classical vs. Neural Planning Trade-offs

  • Explanation: Classical planning is explicit and verifiable but brittle; LLM planning is implicit, flexible, but prone to hallucination and execution drift.
  • Evidence: Comparison of STRIPS/PDDL state representations against LLM generated natural language text.
  • Practical implication: Hybrid approaches combining programmatic structures with neural flexibility are often optimal.

Separating Planner from Executor

  • Explanation: Decomposing tasks into planning modules and execution modules allows the use of specialized models and better optimization.
  • Evidence: SayCan and related vision-only web agents separate high-level planning from low-level grounding.
  • Practical implication: Use strong reasoning models for planning and specialized models or APIs for execution.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Classical Planning (STRIPS)

  • How it works:
  • Components:
    • States (predicates)
    • Actions
    • Preconditions
    • Effects
    • Goal state
  • When to use: When environment dynamics are fully known and verifiable logical correctness is required.

Code-Based Agentic Workflows

  • How it works:
  • Components:
    • Developer-defined procedure
    • Fixed list of actions/vendors
    • Model calls
    • Conditional execution
  • When to use: When tasks require structured, repeatable, and inspectable execution steps.

Multi-Agent Manager-Worker Framework

  • How it works:
  • Components:
    • Manager
    • DAG (Dependency Graph)
    • Parallel CUA Sub-agents
    • Follow-up/Replan loop
    • Summary/Deliverables
  • When to use: For complex, long-horizon tasks requiring specialized capabilities and parallelization.

Examples & Case Studies

An agent tasked with buying a GPU workstation iterates through multiple vendor sites, checks compatibility on a wiki, and handles supply chain lead time failures.

  • Illustrates: The necessity of reactive planning and re-planning when initial vendor options prove suboptimal.
  • Lesson: Agents cannot rely solely on upfront linear plans and must adapt to real-world feedback.

Applying Cursor Plan Mode to a software engineering task to generate a markdown checklist before implementation.

  • Illustrates: Human-in-the-loop plan review and editing before execution.
  • Lesson: Planning mode helps agents gather context and allows human verification, reducing expensive mistakes.

Evaluating multi-agent versus single-agent performance on OSWorld and WebTailBench.

  • Illustrates: Stronger manager models significantly improve coordination and boost the success rate of weaker worker models.
  • Lesson: Modularity and delegation can lift overall system performance without excessive cost increases.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Incorporate task decomposition and step-by-step reasoning in agent prompts.
    • Use plan modes or structured checklists to allow human oversight before agent execution.
  • Strategic:
    • Balance upfront planning with reactive re-planning based on environmental feedback.
    • Adopt modular multi-agent architectures (manager-worker) to handle complex, long-horizon tasks.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • When is planning worth the additional token compute cost?
    • How can we prevent multi-agent handoffs from dropping critical context?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Overthinking in reasoning models correlates with lower issue resolution across benchmark datasets. (empirical research finding)
  • Adding a manager agent to weaker worker models lifts task success rates significantly on web navigation benchmarks. (empirical research finding)

Notable Quotes

"A plan is an explicit representation of intended future behavior: the actions or subgoals an agent will attempt, with any ordering or dependencies among them." (at 19:59) "Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth." (at 22:04)

Compressed Summary

  • Planning structures future agent behavior and enables task decomposition.
  • Chain-of-thought acts as a foundational form of LLM planning.
  • Modularity and separation of planner from executor improve web and robotic task success.
  • Multi-agent manager-worker frameworks help coordinate long-horizon tasks.
  • Keywords: planning, task decomposition, multi-agent, chain-of-thought, modularity
  • Core insight: Effective AI agent design requires balancing structured planning and task decomposition with flexible re-planning and environmental feedback.

  - Separating planners from executors allows specialized model training.
  - Re-planning lets models adapt when execution reveals new information.
- **Examples**:
  - SayCan affordance modeling and Voyager/Odysseys multi-agent architectures.
- **Terminology**:
  - Modularity
  - Affordances
  - Value Functions
  - Re-planning
  - Execution Horizon
  - Overthinking
- **Why it matters**: Structuring agents with modularity and re-planning improves success rates on long-horizon tasks.
### Multi-Agent Coordination and Failures
- **Explanation**: Analyzing multi-agent systems, fixed roles, handoffs, and long-horizon failure modes.
- **Key claims**:
  - Stronger manager agents improve coordination and lift weaker workers.
  - Fixed multi-agent roles can suffer from rigid communication and context drops.
- **Examples**:
  - Vending-Bench long-horizon task failures and OSWorld ablation studies.
- **Terminology**:
  - Multi-Agent Coordination
  - Handoffs
  - Long-Horizon Failures
  - Vending-Bench
- **Why it matters**: Identifies the limitations and pitfalls of multi-agent delegation and execution over extended periods.
## Key Points
### Planning is a moving target
- **Explanation**: Agents must balance commitment to a course of action with flexibility to adapt to new environmental information.
- **Evidence**: Agent tasks in dynamic environments like web browsing require continuous plan revision.
- **Practical implication**: Agent design must incorporate mechanisms for error detection and re-planning.
### Chain-of-Thought acts as a primitive plan
- **Explanation**: Prompting models to think step-by-step or decompose tasks provides a scratchpad and extra compute before final execution.
- **Evidence**: Studies like Least-to-Most Prompting show performance gains from subtask decomposition.
- **Practical implication**: Use structured prompting or decomposition to handle multi-step reasoning tasks.
### Classical vs. Neural Planning Trade-offs
- **Explanation**: Classical planning is explicit and verifiable but brittle; LLM planning is implicit, flexible, but prone to hallucination and execution drift.
- **Evidence**: Comparison of STRIPS/PDDL state representations against LLM generated natural language text.
- **Practical implication**: Hybrid approaches combining programmatic structures with neural flexibility are often optimal.
### Separating Planner from Executor
- **Explanation**: Decomposing tasks into planning modules and execution modules allows the use of specialized models and better optimization.
- **Evidence**: SayCan and related vision-only web agents separate high-level planning from low-level grounding.
- **Practical implication**: Use strong reasoning models for planning and specialized models or APIs for execution.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Classical Planning (STRIPS)
- **How it works**: 
- **Components**:
  - States (predicates)
  - Actions
  - Preconditions
  - Effects
  - Goal state
- **When to use**: When environment dynamics are fully known and verifiable logical correctness is required.
### Code-Based Agentic Workflows
- **How it works**: 
- **Components**:
  - Developer-defined procedure
  - Fixed list of actions/vendors
  - Model calls
  - Conditional execution
- **When to use**: When tasks require structured, repeatable, and inspectable execution steps.
### Multi-Agent Manager-Worker Framework
- **How it works**: 
- **Components**:
  - Manager
  - DAG (Dependency Graph)
  - Parallel CUA Sub-agents
  - Follow-up/Replan loop
  - Summary/Deliverables
- **When to use**: For complex, long-horizon tasks requiring specialized capabilities and parallelization.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An agent tasked with buying a GPU workstation iterates through multiple vendor sites, checks compatibility on a wiki, and handles supply chain lead time failures.
- **Illustrates**: The necessity of reactive planning and re-planning when initial vendor options prove suboptimal.
- **Lesson**: Agents cannot rely solely on upfront linear plans and must adapt to real-world feedback.
### Applying Cursor Plan Mode to a software engineering task to generate a markdown checklist before implementation.
- **Illustrates**: Human-in-the-loop plan review and editing before execution.
- **Lesson**: Planning mode helps agents gather context and allows human verification, reducing expensive mistakes.
### Evaluating multi-agent versus single-agent performance on OSWorld and WebTailBench.
- **Illustrates**: Stronger manager models significantly improve coordination and boost the success rate of weaker worker models.
- **Lesson**: Modularity and delegation can lift overall system performance without excessive cost increases.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Incorporate task decomposition and step-by-step reasoning in agent prompts.
  - Use plan modes or structured checklists to allow human oversight before agent execution.
- **Strategic**:
  - Balance upfront planning with reactive re-planning based on environmental feedback.
  - Adopt modular multi-agent architectures (manager-worker) to handle complex, long-horizon tasks.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - When is planning worth the additional token compute cost?
  - How can we prevent multi-agent handoffs from dropping critical context?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Overthinking in reasoning models correlates with lower issue resolution across benchmark datasets. (empirical research finding)
- Adding a manager agent to weaker worker models lifts task success rates significantly on web navigation benchmarks. (empirical research finding)
## Notable Quotes
> "A plan is an explicit representation of intended future behavior: the actions or subgoals an agent will attempt, with any ordering or dependencies among them." (at 19:59)
> "Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth." (at 22:04)
## Compressed Summary
- Planning structures future agent behavior and enables task decomposition.
- Chain-of-thought acts as a foundational form of LLM planning.
- Modularity and separation of planner from executor improve web and robotic task success.
- Multi-agent manager-worker frameworks help coordinate long-horizon tasks.
- **Keywords**: planning, task decomposition, multi-agent, chain-of-thought, modularity
- **Core insight**: Effective AI agent design requires balancing structured planning and task decomposition with flexible re-planning and environmental feedback.
